The [DivergenceScope](.claude/reference/scope/divergence/DivergenceScope.md) display how connected a given file, how much drive and influence it has.  And more importantly.  When we're viewing a spec entry we should also be able to see how much the implementation diverges from the spec, and vice versa when viewing a source file.  So we can see influence, as well as divergence.  We'd also like to be able to see how well defined a given file is.  The spec may have big gaps, or the implementation may have filled in a lot of the blanks.  Obviously we'll need to save all this as part of the prompt we send to calculate all of this.
We should also save divergence reports since they're costly to run.  They should survive restarts of the application.
The reports tab should show a detailed overall assessment of all the factors we've discussed.  It should also show well defined areas and less well defined areas.

use /lib
from /ui/components/inset-panel import InsetPanelScope
from /ui/components/scrollbar import ScrollbarScope

export scope DivergenceScope:
    concept: {DivergenceConcept}

concept DivergenceConcept:
    pitch:
        Shows how far the code and the spec have drifted apart: which parts of
        the spec drove each source file, and how strongly, what each side does
        that the other doesn't account for, and a single score for the whole
        project.

    shape: {DivergenceShape}

shape DivergenceShape:
    description:
        An analysis of the open project, shown in an @{InsetPanelScope} titled
        "Divergence", with a close button. Opening it starts a fresh analysis
        straight away. Closing the panel while it runs stops it. Once an
        analysis is over, an "Analyze again" button in the panel's header starts
        another.

    minimizing:
        Beside the close button, a minimize button, whose tooltip says the
        analysis keeps running, hides the panel without stopping anything: the
        analysis carries on out of sight, and the window beneath can be used
        again. The panel comes back just as it was left, steps or results, from
        the ribbon's activity list while it runs, or from the Analyze Divergence
        command, which brings back a minimized panel rather than starting
        another. Opening another inset panel, such as a file's diff, while the
        divergence panel is showing minimizes it rather than closing it. Only
        closing it stops it.

    files:
        The source files are every file under the code location, codeRoot in
        piton.config.pi, leaving out what Git ignores and anything that isn't
        text. The spec files are every .pi file under the spec location, root in
        piton.config.pi. Paths are shown relative to the project. Each side is
        capped at 400 files, and the panel says when a side was cut short.

    analyzing:
        steps:
            The analysis first runs `piton build` in the project, so the
            compiled spec is up to date. A build that fails doesn't stop the
            analysis; the panel notes that the compiled spec may be out of date.
            Then two agents run at the same time: one analyzes the code, one
            analyzes the spec. While it runs, the panel lists the steps,
            "Building the spec", "Analyzing the code", and "Analyzing the spec",
            each with a spinner while it runs, a tick once done, or a cross and
            why if it failed.

        stream:
            While an agent runs, beneath its step the panel shows the last three
            lines it has streamed, newest last, as they arrive: each a line of
            the harness's raw JSON output, in the editor's monospace font, muted
            and highlighted as JSON, and cut off with an ellipsis rather than
            wrapped. Until its first line arrives, it reads
            "Waiting for the harness…". Once the agent is done or has failed,
            its lines go.

        agents:
            Each agent is a one-off run of the harness in the project, which can
            only read, glob, and search files, never change anything, and keeps
            no session. It streams its output as JSON, a line per event, and its
            reply is the result it finishes with. It is given both lists of
            files, the code and spec locations, and that the compiled spec is in
            the agent directory's reference folder, and replies with nothing but
            JSON.

            The code agent goes through every source file, and for each says
            which spec files drove it or had influence on it, with how strong
            each influence is, from 0 for barely any to 1 for the file being
            written straight from it, and a short note on what it took from it;
            how far the file diverges from the spec, from 0 for doing just what
            the spec describes to 1 for nothing in the spec accounting for it or
            the spec saying otherwise; and a sentence summing up how it
            diverges, or that it doesn't.

            The spec agent goes through every spec file the same way from the
            other side: which source files implement it, and how strongly, how
            far the code diverges from what the file describes, from 0 for all
            of it being built as described to 1 for none of it being built or
            the code doing otherwise, and a sentence summing it up.

        failing:
            An agent that fails, or replies with something that can't be read,
            fails the analysis, and the panel says why. If only one agent fails,
            what the other found is still shown.

    results:
        connections:
            A connection joins a source file and a spec file. Its strength is
            the average of what both agents said of it, or what one said when
            only one mentioned it, from 0 to 1. Connections to files that aren't
            among the source or spec files are left out. A strength of two
            thirds or more is strong, one third or more moderate, and anything
            less weak.

        score:
            The divergence score is the average divergence of every file the
            agents analyzed, source and spec alike, as a whole percentage. A
            file an agent left out isn't counted, and is shown as
            "Not analyzed". The score is shown large in the header, with what it
            means beside it: "Aligned" below 20%, "Drifting" from 20% up to 50%,
            and "Diverged" from 50%, coloured green, amber, and red.

        trees:
            Beneath the header, a switch between "Source" and "Spec" shows that
            side's files as a tree: a row per folder and file, indented by
            depth, folders before files, each sorted by name. A file's row shows
            its name, a small bar for its divergence, coloured as the score is,
            and its divergence as a percentage, or "Not analyzed". The tree
            scrolls with a @{ScrollbarScope}.

            Clicking a file selects it. Beside the tree, the selected file's
            details: its path, divergence, and summary, then its connections to
            files on the other side, strongest first, each with the other file's
            path, a bar as long as the connection is strong, its strength as a
            percentage, whether it is strong, moderate, or weak, and what the
            agents noted of it. Clicking a connection switches to the other tree
            with that file selected and scrolled into view. With nothing
            selected, the details say to select a file. Once the results are in,
            the source file with the highest divergence is selected.

content.text:
The Divergence panel now shows influence, divergence and definition for each file, has a new Report tab with the overall assessment, and saves every report so it survives restarts. Tests pass except the palette test that was already failing. The spec checks and `piton build` ran clean. I haven't looked at the new layout in the running app, and I haven't run it against a real `claude` analysis.

**What the agents are asked for (the prompt).** The agents are now asked for:
- **For each file:** how well defined it is, from 0 to 1. For a spec file, how complete it is; for a source file, how much the spec covers versus what the code made up.
- **Gaps:** for a spec file, what's missing from it; for a source file, what the code filled in on its own.
- **For each connection:** how far that pair of files diverges, in addition to how strong the connection is.
- **For each side as a whole:** an assessment a few sentences long, plus a list of well defined and less well defined areas, each with a reason.

Reports saved by an older version still open; the new fields just show as empty.

**Measures on each file (Source and Spec tabs).** Selecting a file shows:
- **Influence:** how strongly it's connected to the other side. It is calculated so that one strong connection or several weaker ones both count for a lot.
- **Divergence:** labelled "Diverges from the spec" on a source file and "Implementation diverges" on a spec file.
- **Definition:** how well defined it is.
- **The gaps:** listed as "Filled in by the implementation" or "Gaps in the spec".
- **Connections:** each one now also shows how far that pair diverges.

**Saving.** When an analysis finishes, its report is saved to `.suspense/divergence/<time>.json`, including when one agent failed. Opening the panel shows the latest saved report instead of starting a new analysis; if there isn't one, it analyzes straight away. "Analyze again" starts a new analysis, and the header says how long ago the report was made. That folder isn't in `.gitignore`, so reports will show up for git unless you add it.

**Report tab.** It's the first tab shown, before Source and Spec, and it has:
- **Figures:** the overall divergence score, how well defined each side is on average, what share of each side's files have any connection, and how many files are aligned, drifting or diverged.
- **Assessment:** what each agent wrote about the code and about the spec.
- **Well defined / Less well defined:** the areas the agents named, then the five best and five least well defined files.
- **Most diverged:** the five files that diverge most. Clicking a file in any of these lists opens it in its tree.
- **Saved reports:** every earlier report, with its age and score; clicking one shows it.
- **Notes:** any notes from the run, such as an agent failing.

**Spec.** `spec/scope/divergence/index.pi` now covers all of the above, in new `measures`, `tabs`, `report` and `saving` sections. I also updated the Analyze Divergence button's description in `spec/ui/components/ribbon/spec-tab/index.pi`.

**Code.**
- `src/divergence.rs`: the new fields, the calculations, the updated prompt, and saving and loading reports.
- `src/divergence_view.rs`: the Report tab and the new file details.
- `src/main_window.rs`: a test update.

New tests check the merged measures and the saved-report round trip. Another opens the panel again and confirms it shows the saved report without running the agents, and that "Analyze again" saves a second report.
